messages.author: a6ac2c12dce03d1e
messages.subject: Handedness - best practice
parts:
Hi all-

New to actigraphy processing and curious whether folks have advice on best-practices for collecting and processing data from left-handed participants. Eslinger et al. (2011) provide activity cut-points based on whether the device was worn on the right vs. left wrist. They note that:

"...diminished accuracy experienced on the right wrist was likely due to differences in participant handedness; that is, extraneous movements recorded during the activity conditions were more likely to occur on the right wrist (e.g., scratching, adjusting clothing/glasses, hand gestures). However, given small number of left handed participants (n=5), testing of the hypothesis was untenable."

Based on the above, is it advisable to (1) have all participants wear monitors on the left wrist, process using left-wrist cut-points, and control for handedness or (2) have all participants wear monitors on the dominant wrist, process using left-wrist cut-points, and control for handedness? Are there more recent, published standards that take handedness into account?

Zoë

messages.author: 017566be30afa7f3
messages.subject: Re: [GGIR] Handedness - best practice
parts:
Dear Zoe,

Most studies who have used GGIR went for attachment to the non-dominant wrist. I rarely see studies who define wrist attachment without taking into account handedness.

In theory, controlling for body side and/or handedness in the assessment of movement intensity may help a bit. I believe there are some studies who looked at this in relation to average acceleration over a week or within specific standardised activity types in a lab.

However, to account for it on an epoch by epoch bases in a real life recording you should ideally also account for activity type, because the relation between intensity and body side interacts with activity type. That would make it a lot more challenging to implement, and without it you risk not getting beyond a crude general adjustments, which might even decrease rather than increase comparability between study findings.

Another route is to use same threshold across all your participants, and to include body side or handedness as confounder in your statistical analyses. Not perfect either, but maybe easier to justify.

Vincent


Dr. Vincent van Hees | Independent consultant | https://accelting.com/
